summary: JMAP is a JSON-based protocol for mail and related data, and it can send Web Push notifications to clients. This RFC defines how a JMAP server can advertise that it supports authenticating those pushes using VAPID, so clients can tell the notifications really come from their server.

eli5.summary: When your mail app gets a ping saying "new message," you want to know it truly came from your mail service. This gives the service a way to show its ID badge.

questions: how does jmap use vapid for web push
how does jmap rotate vapid keys
subtitle: How a JMAP server advertises the VAPID key that authenticates its Web Push notifications.

tldr.problem: Some push services require the application server to authenticate every push message with VAPID, so a JMAP client needs the server's VAPID public key to pass to the push service.
tldr.mechanism: A server adds the capability urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid to its session object, with an applicationServerKey holding the public key, and signs each push with the matching private key.
tldr.outcome: Clients can discover VAPID support and rotate keys safely, though a race during rotation can cause a push service to reject a PushVerification with 403.

today: RFC 9749 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why JMAP Needs VAPID
sections.content: RFC 8620 (JMAP) lets clients subscribe to events with a protocol compatible with Web Push (RFC 8030). Some push services require the application server to authenticate every push message using VAPID (RFC 8292). To make that work, the client needs the application server's VAPID public key to pass to the push service when it retrieves a new endpoint.
sections.eli5: The post office will only deliver notes from senders it can identify, so your app has to tell it who the real sender is.

sections.title: Discovering and Using the Key
sections.content:
Servers supporting this RFC MUST add a property named urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid to the capabilities object of the JMAP session object. Its value is an object that MUST contain applicationServerKey: the ECDSA public key in uncompressed form (SEC 1, Section 2.3.3), encoded with base64url. Current systems use the P-256 curve. The format was chosen to be compatible with the browser Push API, so the key can be used without transformation.

Every time the server sends a push message to a PushSubscription URL, including StateChange events and PushVerification notifications, it MUST authenticate the POST request using RFC 8292, with a JSON Web Token signed by the private key matching the advertised key. The key MUST be the one advertised when the PushSubscription was created.
sections.eli5: The server posts its ID badge in a public place, and signs every note it sends so the post office can check the signature against the badge.

sections.title: Key Rotation
sections.content:
When the server replaces its VAPID key, it MUST update the sessionState. The client MUST watch the session object for changes to the key and MUST recreate its push subscription when the key changes. The server MAY keep sending pushes with the old key for a transitional period, and at its end MUST destroy subscriptions that use the old key. It MAY send one final StateChange push first, which prompts the client to call PushSubscription/changes and learn the new key.

A race can occur if the key changes after the client refreshed the session but before it calls PushSubscription/set. The push service then rejects the PushVerification with 403 (Forbidden). The client MUST check that the sessionState in the response points to a session with the key it expects. On a mismatch it MAY retry, and MAY destroy the failed earlier subscription.
sections.eli5: When the server gets a new ID badge, your app has to notice and sign up again with the new badge number.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
During rotation, a client might restrict a push subscription to an outdated key while the server signs a PushVerification with the new one. The push service rejects it with 403, and per RFC 8620 the server MUST NOT retry, so the PushVerification is never delivered. The client is responsible for detecting and resolving this.

Advertising the capability reveals only that the server supports VAPID, and adds no new security or privacy risks beyond those of JMAP and Web Push. IANA registered the capability urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid in the "JMAP Capabilities" registry with intended use common.
sections.eli5: If the badge changes at the wrong moment, one message may get turned away, and your app is the one that has to notice and fix it.
